a2974.speaker: Nick Clegg, Meta president of global affairs
a2974.speech: Said in his news briefing that Zuckerberg hoped to help shape President-elect Donald Trump’s administration on tech policy, including AI; Clegg said he was not privy to whether Zuckerberg and Trump discussed the tech platform’s content moderation policies when Zuckerberg was invited to Trump’s Florida resort last week ; “Mark is very keen to play an active role in the debates that any administration needs to have about maintaining America’s leadership in the technological sphere … and particularly the pivotal role that AI will play in that scenario.”

a3012.speaker: Projection published in the journal The Lancet
a3012.speech: According to the projection, the cut in US international aid funding decided by the Trump administration could lead to more than 14 million deaths by 2030, a third of them children.

a3012.speaker: Davide Rasella, co-author of the study and researcher at the Barcelona Institute for Global Health (quoted in a press release)
a3012.speech: “They risk abruptly halting, or even reversing, two decades of progress in the health of vulnerable populations. For many low- and middle-income countries, the resulting shock would be of a scale comparable to that of a global pandemic or a major armed conflict.”

a3012.speaker: International team of researchers (study of 133 countries)
a3012.speech: Retrospectively estimated that USAID-funded programmes averted 91 million deaths in low- and middle-income countries between 2001 and 2021, and modelled that the 83% cut in US funding could lead to more than 14 million extra deaths by 2030, including more than 4.5 million children under five, around 700,000 extra child deaths per year ; According to the researchers, USAID-supported programmes were associated with a 15% reduction in deaths from all causes, and twice that reduction (32%) for children under five.

a3012.speaker: US Government
a3012.speech: Announced the 83% cut in US funding in early 2025.

a3015.speaker: Jonathan Richter, Director of USAID (in Benin)
a3015.speech: Said that the recent survey was conducted by the Institute for Empirical Research in Political Economy (IREEP) ; Asserts that corruption “has become cultural, and therefore considered normal.”

a3015.speaker: IREEP (Institute for Empirical Research in Political Economy) survey
a3015.speech: Found that 35% of Beninese believe it is no longer possible to eradicate corruption because for them it is a lost cause from the start, and that only 5% of victims of the scourge dare to report acts of corruption, most often out of fear of reprisals.

a3015.speaker: Jean-Baptiste Elias, President of Fonac (Front of National Organisations against Corruption)
a3015.speech: Cited a dozen major corruption cases in Benin for which his institution has gathered evidence over the years so that the perpetrators would be punished, but said political ill will continues to slow matters down, including within the justice system. “We realise, alas, that corruption is not receding as we would have wished; the investigations have made it possible to see that it is impunity that provides the bed for corruption” ; Said that impunity will necessarily have to be fought for corruption to recede or cease in Benin.

a3015.speaker: Jean-Baptiste Elias, President of Fonac
a3015.speech: “The essential thing is that we succeed in bending the trends of these scourges so as to progressively reduce their scale, failing complete eradication” ; Hopes that this 11th national day against corruption will help breathe new dynamism into the fight, whose ultimate aim is to build a prosperous Benin rid of corruption, impunity and all practices that undermine ethics and morality.

a3015.speaker: Fonac officials (organisers of the national anti-corruption day)
a3015.speech: Drew attention to the phenomenon of corruption, which resists all efforts to eradicate it, and said they believe education and governing by example may be the way out.

a3015.speaker: Some participants at the anti-corruption day
a3015.speech: Envisaged a revision of certain texts of the Republic that help to fight corruption but whose application remains difficult.

a3268.speaker: Joseph Boakai, President of Liberia
a3268.speech: Expressed profound thanks and heartfelt gratitude to the people of Liberia for their unwavering commitment to the peace and stability of the country, and said that a year after the historic transition Liberia faces a "MOMENT OF TRUTH" in which democracy can be threatened by those who oppose steady progress; assured that "the security of the state and the sanctity of our Republic, though may be assailed, may be threatened; however, it can never be broken. It will be preserved." ; "No one's ambition can ever outweigh the importance of our peace and security! This rescue train is moving, and I urge those harboring mental reservations to hop on board and let us proceed with the business of the Liberian people together."

a3268.speaker: Joseph Boakai, President of Liberia
a3268.speech: Commended the Fifty-Fifth Legislature for passing eleven legislations and one joint resolution, and urged swift action on outstanding proposals including the Presidential Transition Bill, the National Tourism Bill and the Local Government Bill, the Bank-Financial Institutions and Bank-Financial Holding Companies Act of 2024, the new Zoning Law, the Liberia Youth Service Program (LYSEP) and the TVET Commission Act of 2024; announced he would submit the Amended Payment Systems Act, the Liberia Insurance Regulatory Commission Act, the Revised Code of Conduct for Public Officials and the creation of the State-Owned Enterprises Authority of Liberia (SEAL), warning that "Delays in acting on them could jeopardize the success of the ARREST Agenda for Inclusive Development (AAID)." ; said the government issued 14 Executive Orders in the year under review, including those establishing the Office of War and Economic Crimes Courts (WECC) and the National Railway Authority, and called for strengthened cooperation and dialogue across all branches of government.

a3268.speaker: Joseph Boakai, President of Liberia
a3268.speech: Said the administration inherited an economy in steep decline, with growth slowed to 4.6 percent, inflation at 10.1 percent, a current account deficit of 26.4 percent of GDP, reserves at 2.1 months of import cover and debt of $2.5 billion or 54.6 percent of GDP; reported that in 2024 the economy grew at a revised real GDP rate of 5.1%, driven by mining, agriculture, fisheries and services and supported by international partners such as the World Bank, the African Development Bank, the European Union and USAID; that inflation was reduced to 7.7% and is expected to fall to 6.0% in 2025; that international reserves improved to US$458.9 million, the Liberian dollar appreciated 4.7%, the monetary policy rate was cut from 20% to 17% and private sector credit rose 9.1%; that financial inclusion now covers 52% of the adult population; that the 2025 national budget of US$880.7 million was passed before the start of the fiscal year for the first time in the post-war period; that pump prices for PMS fell 12.53% from $4.47 to $3.91; that total revenue of just over $734 million was collected with domestic revenue of $695.3 million, a 12% growth and the highest in the nation's history, against expenditure of US$661.4 million; that VAT was introduced in April 2024 to replace the GST; and that negotiations with major multinational companies are expected to bring over $3 billion in investments, with medium-term growth of 5.8% in 2025.

a3268.speaker: Joseph Boakai, President of Liberia
a3268.speech: Said his government has worked tirelessly to rebuild trust with international financial institutions and the donor community, securing a US$210 million financing package from the IMF's Extended Credit Facility for 2024-2027, $60 million in World Bank support (US$40 million budget support and US$20 million for a Special Disaster Fund) with a further $40 million pledged for this year and 2026, a $60 million European Union grant for 2025-2027 and $40 million from the African Development Bank for road projects, along with $398.2 million in off-budget Official Development Assistance; and reported "a commitment from the Government of the United States for Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC) Compact eligibility," which he called a significant achievement reflecting confidence in Liberia's transparency, sound economic decisions and governance.

a3268.speaker: Joseph Boakai, President of Liberia
a3268.speech: Reported that the new national development plan and fifteen County Development Agendas have been developed and validated by stakeholders, endorsed by the Cabinet, the National Steering Committee and international partners, and launched on January 15, 2025 as the ARREST Agenda for Inclusive Development (AAID), built on the Pro-Poor Agenda for Prosperity and Development and the Agenda for Transformation and set to cap Vision 2030; said the agenda aims to drive economic transformation through diversification focused on agriculture, road development and infrastructure, the rule of law, improved governance and anti-corruption, and investment in human capital, at a total estimated cost of $8.4 billion, 60 percent of it from government and international donors and the remainder from private investment.

a3268.speaker: Joseph Boakai, President of Liberia
a3268.speech: Said the state of the Republic cannot be spoken of only in terms of "bread and butter" issues and that the country must go beyond policy to address deeper social and political dynamics, including historical social cleavages that divide the nation; said divisions based on religion, social status, literacy and illiteracy, gender and politics must not be allowed to determine how Liberians live, and that "Having come from a difficult past, we must seek to reconcile as a people and embark on nation-building, with a common national aspiration to serve as guardrails against social tensions and conflicts."

a3387.speaker: Alexandre Ngoragoze, provincial secretary of the ruling CNDD-FDD party
a3387.speech: Called on the Bagumyabanga to vote for the CNDD-FDD party in the upcoming elections of 5 June 2025, while also advocating peace and security during this electoral period; recalled that the country is going through a special moment, the national electoral campaign running until 2 June, a moment to raise awareness of the ruling party's achievements since 2005 ; "Our objective is that all 23 deputy seats for the province of Bujumbura come from the CNDD-FDD party. The same goes for the communal councillors. Do you agree?" ; added that every effort must be made to win the elections of 5 June with 96%.

a3387.speaker: Alexandre Ngoragoze, provincial secretary of the ruling CNDD-FDD party
a3387.speech: Presenting the party's programme for society, said the CNDD-FDD will continue to deploy greater efforts in various sectors of the country's life, notably the growth of the national economy, education, good governance, health and the strengthening of diplomacy, and called on the population of the locality to vote for the party.

a3387.speaker: Alexandre Ngoragoze, provincial secretary of the ruling CNDD-FDD party
a3387.speech: Urged CNDD-FDD members to behave well during the electoral period, particularly by advocating peace and security, reminding them that in this period members must consider themselves as a pregnant woman, who adopts particular behaviour so that her embryo does not run into problems ; "At present, the major fight that remains for us is to fight for the development of the country," reassuring the Bagumyabanga that, just as the war of guns has ended, the fight against poverty will without doubt also be won: "Let nothing make us forget the painful past our country has gone through. Since we have peace, our future is promising. What we do not have today, we will have. Let us remain vigilant; let us build our country together."

a3387.speaker: Zenon Ndaruvukanye, member of the Council of Elders of the CNDD-FDD party
a3387.speech: Centred his message on increasing production, calling on the population of the locality to produce a great deal, notably food and export crops, in order to have food and foreign currency; on good governance, he also called on members of the ruling party to choose the CNDD-FDD in order to perpetuate the achievements of the CNDD-FDD and above all the vision of emergence and development of the country.

a3456.speaker: Lieutenant General Matthew Mkingule, Tanzania's High Commissioner to Zambia
a3456.speech: Reaffirmed Tanzania's commitment to maintaining close business relations with Zambia; says that with the conducive environment created by government, the two countries will ensure that business is enhanced; addressing journalists at Kenneth Kaunda International Airport during the arrival of the first ever Air Tanzania Boeing 767 cargo plane, said Zambians should take advantage of the cargo plane and that the Tanzanian government through Air Tanzania will strive to give best incentives to Zambians: "It is good news for the business community. Those who want to import and export products within Africa and beyond Africa. Tanzania will help to link Zambia to the outside world through air transportation. The significance of this air cargo transport is that it is going to facilitate importation and exportation of goods."

a3456.speaker: Lieutenant General Matthew Mkingule, Tanzania's High Commissioner to Zambia
a3456.speech: Said there is need to foster tourism amongst African countries — as much as African governments are promoting domestic tourism, it is prudent that governments promote inter country tourism — and that by so doing African governments will boost economies and create employment for its citizens thereby uplifting livelihoods; added that the African Continental Free Trade Area poses as a good platform to help develop African economies, and said Africa can only develop if African countries support each other.

a3608.speaker: Olaf Scholz (German Chancellor) and Keir Starmer (British Prime Minister) (joint communiqué)
a3608.speech: “Germany and the United Kingdom are bound by a firm friendship and by common values and interests. We are allies in Europe and in NATO and in the face of other challenges, and it is time to raise our relations to another level,” states a joint communiqué from the two leaders.

a3608.speaker: Olaf Scholz, German Chancellor
a3608.speech: In a joint appearance, observed that this will be the first treaty of its kind between Germany and the United Kingdom. The chancellor also referred to Starmer's announcement that he wants to improve relations between the United Kingdom and the EU and said he was pleased with the friendly attitude of the new London government, led by Labour. “The historic decision to leave the EU was taken by the British and this is not about revoking ‘Brexit’. It is about achieving the best possible relations for the benefit of the parties,” said Scholz.

a3608.speaker: Keir Starmer, British Prime Minister
a3608.speech: recalled that Germany is the United Kingdom's second-largest trading partner and that, with an intensification of cooperation, more jobs can be created in both countries. He also said he hoped the treaty would be ready by the end of this year, in order to clarify the terms of the agreement, which addresses bilateral questions but which can also be a start to improving relations between the United Kingdom and the EU.

a3608.speaker: Keir Starmer, British Prime Minister
a3608.speech: said that, with regard to the fight against illegal immigration, the fundamental thing will be cooperation to dismantle human trafficking networks.

a3608.speaker: Keir Starmer, British Prime Minister, and Olaf Scholz, German Chancellor
a3608.speech: reiterated their commitment to helping Ukraine resist the Russian invasion and said that this assistance would continue for as long as necessary.

a3608.speaker: Olaf Scholz, German Chancellor
a3608.speech: “It is important to me to reiterate this because lately people have wanted to give the impression that Germany will reduce its aid. This is not the case,” Scholz assured.

a3608.speaker: Keir Starmer, British Prime Minister
a3608.speech: “We owe a debt to Ukraine. They are fighting for themselves, they are defending themselves, but they are also fighting for all the peoples of Europe,” Starmer added.

a3608.speaker: Keir Starmer, British Prime Minister, and Olaf Scholz, German Chancellor
a3608.speech: addressed the situation in the Middle East and, after underlining that Israel has the right to defend itself, called for access for humanitarian aid to Gaza and for the intensification of efforts to achieve a ceasefire.

a3627.speaker: Gladys Chihozhwa, buyer of medicine at the Hopley market
a3627.speech: She knows the drugs might be expired, or even fake. That doesn't deter her. "I buy them because they are cheap," she says.

a3627.speaker: Medicines Control Authority of Zimbabwe
a3627.speech: In January discovered counterfeit rabies vaccines in circulation, whose packaging mimicked that of legitimate imports from India.

a3627.speaker: United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (2022 report)
a3627.speech: In sub-Saharan Africa alone, counterfeit medicines kill just over a quarter of a million people each year.

a3627.speaker: Grant Marewanhema, public health expert
a3627.speech: Says that even when not immediately fatal, counterfeit medicines can cause long-term harm, including increasing antibiotic resistance.

a3627.speaker: Davison Kaiyo, public relations officer, Medicines Control Authority of Zimbabwe (written response)
a3627.speech: Says the Medicines Control Authority of Zimbabwe has tried to address this problem by conducting raids with the police and intercepting counterfeit medicines at borders, and that they also conduct regular inspections at pharmacies; those caught are prosecuted, and the medicines confiscated, he says.

a3627.speaker: Pacific Research Institute (2020 study)
a3627.speech: Estimated that the counterfeit medicine market is worth somewhere between US$200 billion and US$431 billion annually.

a3627.speaker: World Health Organisation
a3627.speech: 42 percent of globally detected cases of counterfeit and substandard medical products between 2013 and 2017 were in Africa.

a3627.speaker: Portifa Mwendera, pharmacist of 25 years
a3627.speech: Says many public hospitals simply don't have medicine supply; most times, patients are given prescriptions and told to source the medication elsewhere, he says ; says many people in the country are too strapped for cash, and these vendors offer options that are easier on the pocket.

a3627.speaker: Sanudi (middle name used), cross-border truck driver who smuggles medicine
a3627.speech: It's easy, he says. At the border, if the bag is small, he leaves it with a security guard as the truck undergoes scanning; he pays the guard US$50 to US$60, then charges the traders about US$200 to transport two small bags, and if the consignment is too big to stash with the guards, he simply bribes the officials scanning the trucks. "It's a risky operation, but I do it for the extra money I get," he says.

a3627.speaker: Zimbabwe Revenue Authority
a3627.speech: Did not respond to interview requests.

a3627.speaker: Gozo, unlicensed pharmaceutical vendor
a3627.speech: Says that once the customer describes their symptoms, she knows what to sell them, and that two years in this trade have sufficiently equipped her, especially in prescribing antibiotics ; "The people I sell the drugs to get better," she says ; "I always take the risk," she says.

a3801.speaker: Global Financial Integrity (GFI)
a3801.speech: Classifies the movement of money or capital from one country to another as an illicit flow when the funds are illegally earned, transferred, and/or utilized ; reported that efforts to monitor the trillions of dollars of financial transfers flowing through United States banks every year have never been more rigorous and sophisticated ; according to Global Financial Integrity, the only comfort may lie in the fact that United States authorities have not increased their 2015 estimate that domestic financial crime, excluding tax evasion, generates approximately $300 billion of proceeds each year for potential laundering.

a3801.speaker: United States Treasury Department, 2018 report "National Strategy for Combatting Terrorist and Other Illicit Financing"
a3801.speech: Its message is that our security is at risk; it shows that threats are probably escalating, while the responses by law enforcement worldwide are inadequate ; reveals that ISIS, for example, continues to raise funds to support terrorism, obtaining money from selling stolen oil, extorting funds from the people whose villages and towns it controls, the proceeds of crime as well as from United States citizens ; acknowledges that United States banks "generally may be unwitting and can encounter difficulties in identifying the underlying illicit actors given the information available to them" ; states that major efforts are being made to strengthen intelligence sharing across the key departments of the United States government and foreign governmental counterparts.

a3801.speaker: Frank Vogl, co-founder of Transparency International and author of "Waging War on Corruption: Inside the Movement Fighting the Abuse of Power"
a3801.speech: Stated that the various state-sponsored networks, terrorist groups, perpetrators of large-scale cross-border fraud, including cyber crime, as well as drug-trafficking and other criminal organizations might be directed from headquarters beyond United States borders; however, many of their financial transactions go through the United States capital market and are skilfully processed through United States banks.

a3801.speaker: Professor Louise Shelley, George Mason University, author of "Dark Commerce - How a New Illicit Economy is Threatening Our Future"
a3801.speech: Her research shows the deepening international ties between corrupt governments and organized crime, whose joint activities range from vast trafficking in people to ivory and counterfeit goods of all kinds ; both Professor Louise Shelley and the United States Treasury underscore that the uses of crypto-currencies in illicit finance is increasing and placing an even greater challenge on detection and law enforcement.

a3801.speaker: The Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN)
a3801.speech: Estimates that, over the last two years, virtual currency transactions include over 1 billion dollar in ransoms are extortion funds; in addition, over 1.5 billion dollar has been stolen through hacks of virtual currency exchangers and administrators.

a3801.speaker: Moises Naim, journalist, author of "ILLICIT - How Smugglers, Traffickers and Copycats are Hijacking the Global Economy" (2005)
a3801.speech: Wrote a powerful book adding enormous detail about the world of fake products, from medicines and pesticides, to cigarettes and luxury goods of all types.

a3801.speaker: Maya Forstater, visiting fellow at the Center for Global Development
a3801.speech: Asserted that an important step in the right direction will be seen in coming weeks with legislation to be advanced in the United States Congress, whose intent is to provide the United States Treasury with powers to obtain comprehensive knowledge of the true beneficial owners of all holding companies investing in the United States, from those registered in the United States, British Virgin Islands and other offshore centers ; according to Maya Forstater, the legislation, promoted by The Fact Coalition, comprising more than 100 interest groups, has bi-partisan support and, significantly, the backing of leading banking associations who see it as a means of reducing their most substantial regulatory compliance costs.

a3801.speaker: Maya Forstater, visiting fellow at the Center for Global Development
a3801.speech: Seriously stressed that policymakers and the media, not just in the United States, but worldwide, need to wake up to the fact that the scale of illicit finance, and all the crimes it reflects, are a matter of the highest national security priority; unless there is this appreciation, the problems and the threats will multiply.

a3862.speaker: Rohey John Manjang, Minister of Environment, Climate Change and Natural Resources of The Gambia
a3862.speech: said there was the need for Africa to devise homegrown solutions to its challenges. She stated her ambition to build a waste treatment plant in The Gambia within six months through a Public Private Partnership (PPP) arrangement ; “I know, for Africa to go forward with our limited resources, we need to be innovative in making sure that we fix our problems. We cannot just say that we do not have money.” ; “governments cannot do things alone and must bring the private sector on board” ; “…that was why I set for myself a 6-months target that up to June, to build a waste management unit with PPP for The Gambia.”

a3862.speaker: Rohey John Manjang, Minister of Environment, Climate Change and Natural Resources of The Gambia
a3862.speech: assured that the signing of the MoU marked the beginning of a concrete roadmap for implementing a comprehensive waste management solution for the Gambia ; “What we saw this past three days was amazing; it broke our heart for the simple reason that I could not have imagined the solution that the Western countries and institutions proposed with its inherent debt was right here with us in Africa, which does not require much feasibility because this is an African made solution” ; commended the Jospong Group for their innovative approaches and highlighted the Group's comprehensive and entrepreneurial spirit.

a3862.speaker: Dr Joseph Siaw Agyepong, Executive Chairman of the Jospong Group (JGC)
a3862.speech: attributed the progress of his group to divine orchestration. He shared his encounter with the Vice President of The Gambia, which led to the MoU signing ; “When ideas marry strategy, the product is money, so money is the son of strategy and ideas. What we need in Africa is ideas and strategy, not money.”

a3862.speaker: Dr Joseph Siaw Agyepong, Executive Chairman of the Jospong Group (JGC)
a3862.speech: emphasized that Africa's reliance on foreign aid had hindered its progress. He cautioned “If over the years, we've been happy with grants and loans, today Donald Trump has told us that we should go and develop our minerals.” He encouraged Africa to take charge of its development, citing examples of countries like Rwanda that had made significant progress through determination and innovation. He expressed optimism about the project's potential for success in The Gambia, urging Gambians to work together to achieve their goals.

a3902.speaker: Obock delegation members (visitors to Ali-Sabieh)
a3902.speech: Expressed their enthusiasm at having taken the new electric train for their journey to Ali-Sabieh.

a3902.speaker: Charmake Hassan Allaleh, President of the Ali-Sabieh regional council
a3902.speech: “It is an immense pleasure and a great pride that I welcome you today to Ali-Sabieh to celebrate these historic moments of rapprochement and of the signing of the twinning agreement between our two regions: Hayyu and Ali-Sabieh. Your presence here symbolises not only a rapprochement between our regions, but also a shared commitment to a shared future. This twinning marks the beginning of an enriching cooperation focused on the harmonious and sustainable development of our respective territories. Together we have clear ambitions such as strengthening our ties through solidarity, exchange, and the promotion of socio-economic, cultural and tourism development with the aim of improving the living conditions of our fellow citizens.”

a3902.speaker: Mohamed Houmed Ismael, President of the Obock regional council
a3902.speech: Said he was filled with immeasurable joy, as were the members of his delegation, he stressed; thanked the regional authorities and all the people of Ali-Sabieh and Obock for their warm and fraternal welcome; said these visits made to one region and the other will make it possible to seal a fraternal rapprochement and good collaboration between the populations of the two regions.

a3902.speaker: Mohamed Warsama Dirieh, Minister of Trade and Tourism
a3902.speech: Described the event as commendable and imbued with fraternity, symbolising a new stage of cooperation, development and the strengthening of ties between the regions for the well-being of all their inhabitants; said the twinning is much more than a partnership, it is testimony to a shared vision of development built on complementarity, the spirit of solidarity and shared prosperity, and that by working together, Obock and Ali-Sabieh will contribute not only to their own development but also to that of the entire country.

a3902.speaker: Haroun Kassim Ali, Minister Delegate in charge of Decentralisation
a3902.speech: Described this twinning agreement as the fruit of joint reflection and shared will, marking the beginning of a new era of cooperation, solidarity and sustainable development for the two regions; said the twinning is not merely an administrative act but represents the reflection of a clear and ambitious vision that will seal the rapprochement of communities and foster economic, cultural and social exchanges, strengthening fraternal ties and the sense of belonging to one and the same nation; drawing inspiration from Nelson Mandela's statement “Alone we go faster, together we go further”, and calling it a perfect demonstration of the policy of national decentralisation as defined in accordance with the political orientations of the President of the Republic, Ismail Omar Guelleh.

a3998.speaker: Nicole Gbaguidi, State Auditor and staff representative of the former IGE
a3998.speech: Praised the exceptional professional and managerial qualities that Alidou Koussé demonstrated during his time at the head of the IGE, created in 2006 ; recalled the actions and reforms to the outgoing Inspector General of State's credit, placing particular emphasis on the management tools developed by the Inspectorate to give public bodies and enterprises a compass in matters of management ; stressed that today the former IGE shines more brightly than in the past.

a3998.speaker: Alidou Koussé, outgoing Inspector General of State
a3998.speech: Reported that from 2011 to 2015, 2,010 interventions were carried out in the field in the area of management control of public structures and enterprises ; stressed that these results could have been better had financial means not sometimes been lacking ; specified that his institution is not authorised to publish the reports of its field investigations, but that these are regularly transmitted to the Head of State ; expressed his joy at handing over to Auditor General Michel Dognon, whom he knows well and with whom he worked when Dognon was Special Adviser to the Head of State on the governance of public enterprises.

a3998.speaker: Michel Dognon, Auditor General of Benin
a3998.speech: Said it is with pride that he takes the baton from his senior in the profession of accountant, auditor and controller, recalling that Alidou Koussé was his former teacher at the Coulibaly High School in Cotonou and at the National University of Benin and that the two have family ties ; thanked the Head of State for the confidence placed in him since 2014 ; shared with the audience his roadmap for the coming years, saying that corruption is the only threat weighing on the country's development and that he is ready to tackle this national scourge seriously ; committed to strengthening management control within public structures and placing emphasis on preventive auditing and performance auditing in order to limit fraud, over-invoicing and other acts of poor governance ; his roadmap also provides for increasing the Office's staff to 200 agents and creating four regional offices.

a3998.speaker: Lionel Zinsou, Prime Minister of Benin
a3998.speech: Praised the intellectual and professional assets of Michel Dognon, who has already successfully proved himself in the United States of America, a country with a tradition of investigating, monitoring and sanctioning the perpetrators of corruption ; warned the Auditor General that the task will not be easy given the level of corruption in Benin ; “Good governance is not an option. It is binding on everyone” ; invited the Auditor General above all to emphasise the prevention of corruption and the performance of public enterprises ; advised the Office of the Auditor General to work hand in hand with the justice system in order to truly eradicate impunity in Benin.

a4037.speaker: Alousseni Sanou, Malian Minister of Economy and Finance
a4037.speech: Maintains that the unemployment rate has fallen, and fallen considerably, from 6.1% to 3.5% between 2020 and 2024; says the treasury is doing well and that the macroeconomic figures are in the green, so there is nothing to worry about.

a4037.speaker: INSTAT (National Institute of Statistics of Mali), EMOP report, second round 2024
a4037.speech: Data estimate the unemployment rate at 5% in 2024, contrary to Minister Sanou's assertion.

a4037.speaker: Alousseni Sanou, Malian Minister of Economy and Finance
a4037.speech: Said that by multiplying by four the 28 billion subsidy granted to the private sector Guarantee Fund, 150 billion in credit was injected into the economy plus a bonus of 17,000 jobs, and that thanks to the World Bank's PAFM (Mali Access to Finance Project) the State was able to create "roughly 17,286 jobs."

a4037.speaker: Alousseni Sanou, Malian Minister of Economy and Finance
a4037.speech: Said that Mali records the second-best inflation rate in the sub-region, at 3.2%.

a4037.speaker: African Development Bank (AfDB)
a4037.speech: Reports that Mali's inflation fell from 9.7% in 2022 to 2.2% in 2023, under the combined effect of the BCEAO's restrictive monetary policy, uninterrupted supply of local markets and the 25% customs duty exemption granted by the government in exchange for ceiling prices on sugar; and projects growth of 4.7% in 2024 and 5.3% in 2025, driven by extractive activities including the start of lithium production, the revival of the textile sector and wheat production, with inflation continuing to fall to 2% in 2024 and 1.8% in 2025.

a4037.speaker: Monthly statistical bulletin of the Central Bank of West African States (BCEAO)
a4037.speech: Shows that in February 2025 Mali posted the highest inflation rate in the WAEMU, at 8.3%, up from 7.6% in January 2025 and well above the central bank's target range of 1% to 3%.

a4037.speaker: WAEMU Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP) report
a4037.speech: Attributes the rise in inflation to price increases for "food products and non-alcoholic beverages (8.2%), housing, water, electricity, gas and other fuels (11.4%), restaurant and accommodation services (5.8%), personal care services, social protection and miscellaneous goods (12.5%), as well as information and communication services (9.8%)."

a4037.speaker: Alousseni Sanou, Malian Minister of Economy and Finance
a4037.speech: Announced that during the transition the State subsidised EDM to the tune of 461 billion, Comatex about 2 billion, UMPP about 1.253 billion to manufacture 10 AMO products, the private sector Guarantee Fund 28 billion, and the CMDT 90 billion to support the economy.

a4037.speaker: Alousseni Sanou, Malian Minister of Economy and Finance
a4037.speech: Reiterated that the 2025 State budget was adopted piecemeal by the CNT on 12 and 19 December 2024, estimated at 2,648.900 billion FCFA in revenue and 3,229.886 billion FCFA in expenditure, for a deficit of 580.986 billion FCFA, and that covering the PAG's priorities of around 1,600 billion would require the June amending finance law.

a4037.speaker: Alousseni Sanou, Malian Minister of Economy and Finance
a4037.speech: Announced that all indicators are trending in the right direction and that Mali remains the 4th economy of the Franc zone, behind Burkina Faso.

a4087.speaker: Abiy Ahmed, Prime Minister of Ethiopia
a4087.speech: "To our (Sudanese and Egyptian) brothers; Ethiopia built the dam to prosper, to electrify the entire region and to change the history of black people. It is absolutely not to harm its brothers." ; Has said Ethiopia will use the energy to improve Ethiopians' access to electricity and export surplus power to the region.

a4087.speaker: Ethiopian government
a4087.speech: Says the dam's reservoir, which has flooded an area larger than Greater London, will provide a steady water supply for irrigation downstream while limiting floods and drought; Ethiopia in 2020 began filling the reservoir in phases while arguing that the dam would not significantly harm downstream countries.

a4087.speaker: Tamim Khallaf, Egyptian Foreign Ministry spokesperson
a4087.speech: Told Reuters on Monday that Egypt would continue to closely monitor developments on the Blue Nile and "exercise its right to take all the appropriate measures to defend and protect the interests of the Egyptian people".

a4087.speaker: Egypt (official position)
a4087.speech: Fears the GERD could restrict its water supply during periods of drought, and could lead to the construction of other upstream dams; has bitterly opposed the dam from the start, arguing that it violates water treaties dating to the British colonial era and poses an existential threat.

a4087.speaker: Sudan (official position)
a4087.speech: Has joined Egypt's calls for legally binding agreements on the dam's filling and operation.

a4087.speaker: Independent research
a4087.speech: Shows that so far, no major disruptions to downstream flow have been recorded - partly due to favourable rainfall and cautious filling of the reservoir during wet seasons over a five-year period.

a4087.speaker: Mekdelawit Messay, Ethiopian water researcher at Florida International University
a4087.speech: Said that in Ethiopia, which has faced years of internal armed conflict largely along ethnic lines, the GERD has proven a source of national pride. "It has been a banner to rally under, and it shows what we can achieve when unified."

a4087.speaker: Ethiopian local media (reports)
a4087.speech: Local media has reported that Ethiopia's central bank provided 91% of the project's funding, while 9% was financed by Ethiopians through bond sales and gifts, without any foreign assistance.

a4087.speaker: Sultan Abdulahi Hassan, farmer living near the dam
a4087.speech: Said the dam has brought electricity to his village. "We now have refrigerators. We can drink cold water. We now use electricity for everything," he told Reuters at the launch.

a4087.speaker: World Bank (data)
a4087.speech: According to the World Bank, while urban areas had a 94% electrification rate as of 2022, just 55% of the country's total population had electricity.

a4164.speaker: Sappi (statement)
a4164.speech: “Our Saiccor, Tugela and Stanger Mills along with its export facilities at the Durban Port have been impacted. Production has been stopped, some inventory is damaged, and deliveries to domestic customers have been affected,” said Sappi in a statement on Wednesday ; added that its export shipments would also be affected; said there had been no material damage to its plants, and it has insurance for its property and stock, and that in the meantime the mills will run on a skeleton crew as a precautionary measure until staff can safely return to work.

a4164.speaker: Steve Binnie, Sappi CEO
a4164.speech: “Sappi is deeply saddened by the loss of life and devastating impact of these floods on the people of KwaZulu-Natal. Our condolences go out to the families of those in various communities who have lost loved ones. Over and above support we will be providing in Sappi communities, we will join organised business to provide the necessary support” ; added that Sappi was working on minimising the impact on its customers and that shareholders would be updated on the impact at the three mills once this had been quantified.

a4324.speaker: Dr. Alexander Nuetah, Liberian Agriculture Minister
a4324.speech: Said the government will provide the farmers with all necessary materials for cultivation of the targeted threshold of lowland in Nimba County, urged the people of Nimba County to take ownership of the initiative to help the government reduce the importation of the country’s staple food, rice, and said that as a key component of the Government’s ARREST Agenda for Inclusive Development, agriculture needs a holistic approach to tackle hunger in Liberia; he spoke Wednesday in Garplay, Nimba County, when he met with the Flokwado Farmers’ Cooperative.

a4324.speaker: Dr. Alexander Nuetah, Liberian Agriculture Minister
a4324.speech: Charged the administration of Garplay Public School to formulate a school garden proposal to support the agriculture sector, to be submitted to the Ministry for onward implementation, saying he believes the instrument will empower Garplay Public School and increase food production in Nimba County, and thanked the staff of the school for their continued commitment to providing quality education.

a4393.speaker: Trump administration
a4393.speech: In issuing the executive orders, said the review seeks to assess the efficiency and consistency of US foreign policy under the 'America First' agenda to "realign foreign assistance on behalf of hardworking taxpayers", stating that it is not just the right thing to do, but "a moral imperative".

a4393.speaker: The Nation (January 29 2025 edition)
a4393.speech: Reported that a total of $284.7 million (about K493.7 billion) financing through USAid to Malawi is at stake.

a4393.speaker: Ministry of Finance and Economic Affairs (Malawi)
a4393.speech: Said of the amount, US contribution to the 2024/25 National Budget stood at K9.2 billion of the expected K1.17 trillion projected grants.

a4393.speaker: World Bank Group
a4393.speech: Describes trade as a golden key towards ending global poverty because countries that are open to international trade tend to grow faster, become innovative, improve productivity and provide higher income as well as more opportunities.

a4725.speaker: Kenneth Gilbert Adjei, Minister of Works, Housing and Water Resources of Ghana
a4725.speech: Has called on stakeholders in the water sector to strengthen collaboration and create synergies in their operations for efficient delivery of water services to Ghanaians ; stressed that there was a need for synergy between both state and non-state water sector institutions and agencies because if they did not shake each other, their investments could be duplicated and, therefore, counterproductive ; said in an era when the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) had ceased its investment across the world, affecting some water projects, the state and private sector needed to work closely together to prudently channel resources into water systems that would be of utmost benefit to the people ; "However, we recognise that the government alone cannot solve all the challenges in the water sector. Partnerships with non-state actors such as Safe Water Network, other members of the Safe Water Enterprises (SWE) Alliance, the private sector and development partners are not only welcome but essential."

a4725.speaker: Kenneth Gilbert Adjei, Minister of Works, Housing and Water Resources of Ghana
a4725.speech: Described the theme of the forum as apt and timely because the country was at a critical point where access to water had become a critical development challenge ; said in furtherance of the commitment made by President John Dramani Mahama in his maiden State of the Nation Address to Parliament to expand water access for all Ghanaians, the Works and Water Resources Ministry would implement policies that would accelerate access to the resource, that ongoing water projects would be completed and new ones initiated at both the urban and rural levels "to ensure that every Ghanaian, regardless of where they live, enjoys the right to safe and reliable water" ; stressed that there would be more targeted investment in infrastructure, institutional reforms and digital innovation to drive progress.

a4725.speaker: Gizella Tetteh-Agbotui, Deputy Minister of Works, Housing and Water Resources of Ghana
a4725.speech: Said one of the most challenging issues to access to quality water was the galamsey scourge: "Galamsey has taken over our water quality, and it is pathetic to see how people suffer for water in communities and regions where the menace is rife. We are at a crisis point now, and all of us must play our roles as expected to help save our water bodies." ; touching on the Blue Water initiative in which 400 water guards were deployed to protect rivers, said it was a great move to help bring back heavily polluted water bodies, and contrary to criticisms that the initiative would not make any impact on the galamsey fight, said "the people are taken from the community and they can help to fight galamsey if there is political will to do so" ; "Inter-ministerial and inter-development partner collaborations are key in all of these."

a4725.speaker: Gizella Tetteh-Agbotui, Deputy Minister of Works, Housing and Water Resources of Ghana
a4725.speech: Said as a government that just took over a couple of months back, they were currently assessing water sector projects that had stalled and water systems that were malfunctioning, and collaborating with other state institutions to halt galamsey and other human activities that polluted water sources.

a4725.speaker: Charles Nimako, Country Director of Safe Water Network Ghana and Lead for Africa initiatives
a4725.speech: Highlighted that over the past year, the entity had expanded to an additional 55,000 people in 10 communities across the country, taking their total coverage to 504,000 people in 158 communities ; said when that number was added to what had been achieved by other implementers of water services, particularly Safe Water Enterprise Alliance, then more than two million Ghanaians would be reached with safe and affordable water ; stressed that although that achievement was a key milestone, it was not "the finish line" ; "In the coming months, we will continue to build on the progress we have made by strengthening the technical and financial resilience of our model, equipping local operators and field support teams, and aligning with government priorities as articulated in the President's State of the Nation Address and the 2025 Budget that was delivered in Parliament."

a4807.speaker: Jonathan Bloom, Vice-President of the Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC) for Africa
a4807.speech: Declared that the objective of the memorandum of understanding signed on Thursday is to promote growth. “We are here to move forward still further after the results recorded for the first Compact with respect to access to justice, to land and to finance.” For him, the lack, insufficiency or continued unavailability of electricity remains a major obstacle to growth. “There is a programme being implemented to remedy this,” he indicated, stating that an envelope of 250 million dollars, about 125 billion CFA francs, will be devoted to it. “This will be the solution to these problems; I remain confident that with the leadership of the ministers present here, of the coordinator of the UCF/MCA and of the President of the Republic, the lives of the people will be improved.”

a4807.speaker: Jonathan Bloom, Vice-President of the Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC) for Africa
a4807.speech: Indicated, following the signing of the memorandum, that the agreement in principle settles the institutional and policy framework of the energy sector, which will make it possible in time to increase the supply of electricity for businesses and households in Benin. He remarked that this requires a framework and a regulation of budgetary resources to make investments sustainable, allowing the government to move forward in order to avoid interruptions in the supply of electric power; there will be reforms that will establish and guarantee the sustainability of investments for operational and technical purposes, and it will be more possible to do business in the sector, which was previously lacking. He also explained that the MCC Board of Directors will meet in the meantime to endorse the proposals made by the experts.

a4807.speaker: Komi Koutché, Minister of the Economy, Finance and Denationalisation Programmes of Benin
a4807.speech: “This day is memorable for the Beninese government; I salute our American friends and all the other actors who worked so that we could arrive at these results.” MCA is a trophy, he remarked, going on to say that the first Compact made it possible to shift many lines and that the journey has been long but enriching. “We make the commitment that we will carry out the reforms meticulously and will do everything for them to succeed.”

a4991.speaker: African Policy Research Institute (APRI), report 'Mapping Africa's Green Mineral Partnerships'
a4991.speech: Highlights existing agreements that allow industrialized nations—including the U.S., China, the UK, Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Russia, India, South Korea, and Japan—to extract Africa's resources.

a4991.speaker: General Murtala Muhammed, Nigeria's former Head of State
a4991.speech: Stated in his landmark 1976 speech at the Organization of African Unity (OAU) Summit in Addis Ababa that Africa deserves fair trade, not continued exploitation.

a4991.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a4991.speech: His stance that "every nation should fend for itself."

a4991.speaker: Professor Bolaji Akinyemi, chairman of the council, Nigerian Institute of International Affairs (NIIA)
a4991.speech: At a recent reception at the NIIA he playfully questioned the author's strong support for Trump, and seemed curious about his stance.

a4991.speaker: Magnus Onyibe, entrepreneur, public policy analyst and author of the article
a4991.speech: In response, I explained that, given the difficult path Trump took to reclaim the White House, he appears to be a leader determined to challenge the status quo and, in many ways, "save the world from itself." I ended on a lighthearted note, telling him not to be surprised if a Trump Tower soon becomes part of the skylines of Lagos or Abuja.

a5054.speaker: European Commission (EU executive, press statement)
a5054.speech: According to a statement from the EU executive, an air bridge is being launched to take essential goods to the victims of Typhoon Yagi, with a flight expected to arrive in Laos in the coming days.

a5182.speaker: Somali government spokesman (tweet)
a5182.speech: Posted a misinforming tweet that falsely claimed that the UK's ambassador to Mogadishu discussed a wide range of topics including the current political situation, strengthening relations & cooperation between the two countries, and security & economic cooperation.

a5182.speaker: Kate Foster, UK Ambassador to Somalia (tweet)
a5182.speech: Immediately replied by clarifying the content of discussion during the Sunday meeting, tweeting “Constructive meeting with @KhadarGulaid discussing current political situation. Reaffirmed that the UK will not support term extensions. Emphasised the importance of an urgent return to a consensus-based electoral model.”

a5182.speaker: Western governments (U.S., UK and the European Union)
a5182.speech: Strongly objected to Farmajo's term extension and even vowed to consider “changing” the nature of relations with Somalia, falling short of threatening sanctions.

a5182.speaker: Antony Blinken, US Secretary of State
a5182.speech: Said the US will “re-evaluate” bilateral relations with Somalia if the president forces through the extension.

a5182.speaker: Somali Opposition group the National Salvation Forum and the federal member states of Puntland and Jubbaland
a5182.speech: Warned and boycotted the extension of the president's term and called it “a threat” to Somalia's peace and security.

a5213.speaker: Antonio Guterres, UN Secretary-General
a5213.speech: Said Africa has everything it takes to become a “renewable superpower” and called for greater investment in green energy across the resource-rich continent: “We must mobilize finance and technology, so that Africa's natural wealth benefits African people, we must build a thriving renewables and manufacturing base across the continent.” ; “Green power in Africa lowers energy costs, diversifies supply chains and accelerates decarbonization for everyone.” ; “Africa has everything it takes to become a renewable superpower, from solar and wind to the critical minerals that power new technology.” He also urged greater investment in climate solutions.

a5213.speaker: Antonio Guterres, UN Secretary-General
a5213.speech: Warned in his speech in the Japanese port city of Yokohama that “debt must not drown development” and that Africa needed increased concessional finance and greater lending capacity from multilateral development banks.

a5213.speaker: Lowy Institute, Australian think tank
a5213.speech: Said in May that new lending is drying up, and developing countries are grappling with a “tidal wave” of debt to both China and international private creditors.

a5213.speaker: William Ruto, Kenyan President
a5213.speech: Said on social media platform X that Kenya was in talks with Japanese automaker Toyota for the provision of 5,000 “e-mobility vehicles” as part of the country's “commitment to clean energy.”

a5213.speaker: Shigeru Ishiba, Japan's Prime Minister
a5213.speech: In his opening address at the forum on Wednesday, announced a plan to train 30,000 people in artificial intelligence in Africa over three years and to study the idea of a Japan-Africa Economic Partnership; before the meeting kicked off, he also announced a vision for a distribution network that links African and Indian Ocean nations.

a5213.speaker: Bola Tinubu, Nigerian President, and Cyril Ramaphosa, South African President
a5213.speech: Both said, speaking on X, that they wanted a shift from aid to investment partnerships.

a5298.speaker: Mahamud Farah Beenebeene, Minister of Planning, Investment, and Economic Development of the Federal Government of Somalia
a5298.speech: emphasized Somalia's commitment to sustainable development and highlighted the importance of aligning donor support with national priorities.

a5298.speaker: Federal Government of Somalia
a5298.speech: expressed its gratitude to the UK Government and other international partners for their continued contributions to the country's reconstruction and economic development ; the Government remains committed to working closely with international partners to implement effective policies that foster inclusive and sustainable development.

a5298.speaker: Somali Ministry of Planning and the British Embassy in Somalia (joint)
a5298.speech: Both sides agreed to strengthen cooperation to ensure that all development efforts are well-coordinated, sustainable, and mutually beneficial ; a major point of discussion was the impact of reductions in Official Development Assistance (ODA) funding, with both parties assessing strategies to mitigate potential setbacks.

a5433.speaker: Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC) Board of Directors
a5433.speech: At its quarterly meeting held on 18 September 2024 in Washington, approved Côte d’Ivoire’s regional Compact for fiscal year 2025 to modernise the country’s electricity grid, a five-year programme budgeted at $300 million (about 180 billion FCFA) financed by the MCC plus a $22.5 million (about 13 billion FCFA) contribution from the government of Côte d’Ivoire ; at the same meeting also approved Zambia’s Compact to stimulate inclusive economic growth in the agriculture and agro-industry sectors.

a5433.speaker: Sercom CFPCR-MCC (source of the release)
a5433.speech: Cited as the source of the report on the MCC board decisions and on the MCC’s mandate: created in 2004, the MCC is an independent development agency of the U.S. government working to reduce poverty worldwide through economic growth, granting time-limited subsidies for infrastructure investments and for policy and institutional reforms in countries that meet rigorous standards of good governance, anti-corruption and respect for democratic rights.

a5495.speaker: Medecins Sans Frontieres (MSF) / Doctors Without Borders (statement of Tuesday)
a5495.speech: Announced indefinite reduction of its outreach medical activities in Yei County of Central Equatoria State due to "increased insecurity" ; "Due to increased insecurity, Medecins Sans Frontieres (MSF) has made the difficult decision to reduce outreach activities around Yei, Central Equatoria State, South Sudan until further notice" ; said it is deeply concerned about the impact this reduction will have on vulnerable communities; urged all parties to the conflict to ensure the protection of civilians and guarantee unhindered access to medical and humanitarian assistance for all people.

a5495.speaker: Emmanuel Taban, Commissioner of Yei River County, Central Equatoria State
a5495.speech: Reported that a woman was killed and two others were injured during an attack on a civilian vehicle along the Yei-Umbasi road on Saturday, April 26; said the vehicle was carrying civilian passengers from Yei to Umbasi, and added that the assailants are yet to be identified and arrested; revealed that the perpetrators fled the scene; reassured the public, stating that the situation has returned to normal, and the road is now safe for travel.

a5495.speaker: UN Mission in South Sudan (UNMISS)
a5495.speech: Urged an immediate end to hostilities and restoration of calm in Morobo and Yei counties, Central Equatoria State, following renewed clashes between government forces and the SPLA-IO that displaced thousands of civilians; appealed to the warring factions to refrain from conflict, prioritize the protection of civilians, resolve differences through dialogue, while ensuring unimpeded access for peacekeepers to reinforce security; added that it was engaging with authorities, security actors, faith-based groups, traditional leaders, youths, civil society and community leaders to prevent the situation from deteriorating.

a5538.speaker: Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, Egyptian President
a5538.speech: Has rejected US President Donald Trump's plan to take over Gaza and move Palestinians to Egypt and Jordan; for now, until Trump stops talking about forcing the displacement of Palestinians, el-Sisi has reportedly said that he will not attend any talks at the White House.

a5538.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a5538.speech: Suggested that the United States “take over” the enclave and expel Palestinians to Egypt and Jordan, and threatened that he would freeze aid funds to Egypt if it does not cooperate.

a5538.speaker: Egypt (official statement)
a5538.speech: Hours later, Egypt issued a statement confirming it would present “a comprehensive vision for rebuilding Gaza while ensuring Palestinians remain on their land” and reiterated its commitment to working with the US to reach “a just settlement to the Palestinian issue”.

a5538.speaker: Jacob Eriksson, lecturer of post-war recovery studies at the University of York
a5538.speech: “It’s hard to know how seriously to take Trump’s proposed US takeover of Gaza.” ; “If Trump persists, however, it could put Egypt in a difficult position,” referring to Trump’s threats that he would freeze aid funds to Egypt if it does not cooperate ; “At a time when Egypt continues to face mounting economic challenges linked to debt and inflation, this could have a significant impact.”

a5538.speaker: Jacob Eriksson, researcher, University of York
a5538.speech: “While any significant economic contribution to the reconstruction of Gaza is likely to prove difficult given aforementioned economic challenges, Egyptian officials … would undoubtedly continue to offer its services as a mediator and a political partner,” doubtful of how much Egypt could financially contribute.

a5538.speaker: American Chamber of Commerce in Egypt (figures)
a5538.speech: According to the American Chamber of Commerce in Egypt, since 1946 the United States has given Egypt more than $85bn in bilateral foreign aid, including military and economic assistance.

a5538.speaker: Hossam El-Hamalawy, Egyptian journalist
a5538.speech: Said that the aid Cairo receives “is a statement that Egypt is a close ally and is a partner for Washington” and signifies strong political backing from Washington.

a5538.speaker: Hossam El-Hamalawy, Egyptian journalist
a5538.speech: “Generation after generation of Egyptian youth have had Palestine as their gateway into politics.” ; “In addition … [Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi] is very worried about the replication of the Beirut scenario where Palestinian resistance operations in one way or another gave Israel a justification to go into Lebanon and occupy chunks of it for a very long time.”

a5538.speaker: Hossam El-Hamalawy, Egyptian journalist
a5538.speech: “One can speculate that, definitely, [this plan] will involve enlisting massive amounts of cash and finances from the Gulf … to speed up the reconstruction process for the Palestinians without displacing them.”

a5538.speaker: Abdallah Nasef, political analyst
a5538.speech: “Any drastic action could endanger important agreements.” ; “Egypt could, similar to Jordan, offer to take in injured individuals and their families, albeit at a larger rate and number than that proposed by Jordan.”

a5538.speaker: Abdallah Nasef, political analyst
a5538.speech: “Egypt could contribute to reconstruction efforts while simultaneously guaranteeing that Gazans don’t need to be forced out,” adding that “They won’t have to if caravans and tents, which Israel continues to block, are allowed into the Strip.” He agreed with El-Hamalawy that Egypt’s efforts would have to be bankrolled by the Gulf, due to Egypt’s economic problems.

a5538.speaker: King Abdullah II of Jordan
a5538.speech: Said on Tuesday that Jordan could “right away” take 2,000 sick children.

a5538.speaker: Israel (official position)
a5538.speech: Israel has said that it will not compensate Palestinians or help to pay to fix the damage it has wrought in Gaza; instead, it would be up to regional countries and the international community to implement any plan put forward by Egypt and Jordan.

a5538.speaker: Hisham Talaat Moustafa, Egyptian real estate and construction tycoon
a5538.speech: Said in a TV interview on February 9 that he has been working on a reconstruction plan that would require the participation of about 40 to 50 construction companies from Egypt and other countries.

a5538.speaker: Gulf Cooperation Council (announcement)
a5538.speech: Announced in December that its member states – Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and the United Arab Emirates – had collectively given $650m in humanitarian aid to Gaza, along with the occupied West Bank, since October 2023.

a5766.speaker: John Dramani Mahama, President of Ghana (in his memoir My First Coup d'État)
a5766.speech: Writes of the expulsion of Ghanaian refugees from Nigeria in the 1970s: “Things had come to this. The feeling that life anywhere else, no matter how dangerous it was to get there or how difficult it was to live there, was better than life in Ghana, the home we had all once loved and cherished and had never before dreamt of leaving.”

a5766.speaker: John Dramani Mahama, President of Ghana (in his memoir My First Coup d'État)
a5766.speech: On his family’s relative wealth: “Only a few houses in town, the houses of affluent people were roofed with corrugated iron sheets. Ours was one of them.”

a5897.speaker: Moehler et al. (2014) (study)
a5897.speech: According to Moehler et al. (2014), economic disparities in the Sahel, combined with high unemployment particularly among young people, create fertile ground for radicalisation.

a5897.speaker: Roy (2017) (study)
a5897.speech: Cited for the claim that social exclusion pushes some young people, often without prospects, to seek refuge and meaning in extremist ideologies that promise a more just world and a moral order imposed by Islamic law.

a5897.speaker: Chauzal & Van Damme (2015) (study)
a5897.speech: Cited for the claim that ethnic rivalries in the Sahel are often linked to the management of natural resources, particularly where access to water and farmland is crucial for community survival.

a5897.speaker: Bøås & Dunn (2013) (study)
a5897.speech: Cited for the claim that fragile Sahelian states have seen their legitimacy eroded by a lack of public services, corruption and insufficient protective capacity, so that governments are increasingly perceived as incompetent, opening the way to violent alternatives proposed by terrorist groups exploiting the power vacuum.

a5897.speaker: Vogel (2020) (study)
a5897.speech: According to Vogel (2020), terrorist groups offer not only physical protection but also local justice based on sharia, presented as a more effective and just substitute for state administration perceived as corrupt and inefficient.

a5897.speaker: Mackinlay (2009) (study)
a5897.speech: Cited for the claim that the jihadist narrative of a return to authenticity and struggle against Western imperialism resonates with those who feel excluded and abandoned by the powers in place and the international community.

a5897.speaker: Lacher (2017) (study)
a5897.speech: Cited for the claim that the porous borders between Sahel states, notably in regions such as Liptako-Gourma, allow the free circulation of fighters, weapons and financing.

a5897.speaker: Boukhars (2021) (study)
a5897.speech: Cited for the claim that the persistent instability of neighbouring countries such as Libya and Sudan continues to provide fertile ground for the flourishing of these groups.

a5897.speaker: Human Rights Watch (2019) (report)
a5897.speech: Cited for the claim that the rise in violence has caused massive uprooting of populations and exacerbated humanitarian crises, with millions forced to flee their homes and live in precarious conditions in refugee camps.

a5897.speaker: UNHCR and OCHA (data)
a5897.speech: According to the most recent data from UNHCR and OCHA, more than 5 million people have been displaced in the central Sahel (Burkina Faso, Mali, Niger) since 2019, a constantly rising figure.

a5897.speaker: Unicef (2024) (report)
a5897.speech: Cited for the figure that in Burkina Faso more than 6,000 schools were closed or non-functional in 2024, depriving hundreds of thousands of children of access to education.

a5897.speaker: Raineri (2023); ISS Africa (2024) (studies)
a5897.speech: Cited for the claim that since 2021 attacks have been regularly recorded in northern Benin, Togo, Côte d’Ivoire and even Ghana, raising fears of terrorist contagion towards the Gulf of Guinea countries.

a5897.speaker: IOM (International Organization for Migration) and UNHCR
a5897.speech: Cited as having well documented the link between insecurity and forced migration.

a5897.speaker: Lebovich (2022) (study)
a5897.speech: Cited for the criticism that EU programmes such as the P3S and the EUTF, which aim to “address the root causes” of irregular migration, take an approach that is at times too security-focused to the detriment of long-term development.

a5897.speaker: Galy (2023) (study)
a5897.speech: Cited for the claim that Western withdrawals are often interpreted as a loss of Western influence, leaving the field open to other powers, notably Russia through the Wagner group, which has gained ground in several countries of the region.

a5897.speaker: ICG (International Crisis Group) (2023) (report)
a5897.speech: Cited for the claim that attacks on convoys, sabotage of infrastructure or threats to extraction zones in Niger, an important uranium producer, can have repercussions on energy supply chains.

a5897.speaker: Boutellis & Williams (2023) (study)
a5897.speech: Cited for the call by many academic analyses and international reports for a change of paradigm, favouring integrated approaches based on local development, community reconciliation, social justice and political inclusion.

a5897.speaker: Olivier Roy (2017), cited in the conclusion
a5897.speech: As Olivier Roy (2017) emphasises, it is not enough to kill fighters: the very sources of radicalisation must be dried up, that is, social fractures, exclusion, humiliation and the institutional vacuum.

a6116.speaker: Antoine Gérard, the UN's deputy humanitarian co-ordinator for Sudan
a6116.speech: Said that it was hard to assess the scale of the incident or the exact death toll as the area was very hard to reach.

a6116.speaker: Antoine Gérard, the UN's deputy humanitarian co-ordinator for Sudan
a6116.speech: Said getting aid quickly to the area would be difficult: “We do not have helicopters, everything goes in vehicles on very bumpy roads. It takes time and it is the rainy season - sometimes we have to wait hours, maybe a day or two to cross a valley... bringing in trucks with commodities will be a challenge.”

a6116.speaker: Sudan Liberation Movement/Army (SLM/A) (statement)
a6116.speech: Had earlier said as many as 1,000 people could have died; said in a statement that days of heavy rain triggered the landslide on Sunday, which left just one survivor and “levelled” much of the village of Tarseen.

a6116.speaker: Sudan Liberation Movement/Army (SLM/A)
a6116.speech: Has appealed for humanitarian assistance from the UN and other regional and international organisations.

a6116.speaker: Minni Minnawi, Darfur's army-aligned governor
a6116.speech: Called the landslide a “humanitarian tragedy”: “We appeal to international humanitarian organisations to urgently intervene and provide support and assistance at this critical moment, for the tragedy is greater than what our people can bear alone,” he said in a statement quoted by the AFP news agency.

a6116.speaker: Mahmoud Ali Youssouf, head of the African Union Commission
a6116.speech: Called on the warring parties “to silence the guns and unite in facilitating the swift and effective delivery of emergency humanitarian assistance to those in need”.

a6116.speaker: A US official (unnamed)
a6116.speech: Last year estimated up to 150,000 people had been killed since hostilities began in 2023.

a6357.speaker: Officials of GIABA (Inter-Governmental Action Group against Money Laundering in West Africa)
a6357.speech: According to the institution’s officials, the year 2024 was on the whole a good one, but it was not free of challenges. Although countries have adopted international standards, practical implementation on the ground remains inconsistent and criminals continue to exploit legal persons for the purposes of illicit financial flows.

a6357.speaker: GIABA latest annual report
a6357.speech: According to GIABA’s latest annual report, all these countries are the subject of heightened attention because of their close links with the expansion of the informal economy. ; In many countries of the subregion, again according to this report, legal persons can issue bearer shares, making efforts to trace beneficial owners even more complex. ; The report nonetheless indicates that only Ghana, Nigeria and Senegal currently have a solid beneficial-ownership transparency framework.

a6357.speaker: GIABA (report recommendations to national authorities)
a6357.speech: National authorities are recommended to create and keep up to date registers of beneficial owners accessible to the competent authorities, and to standardise the transparency regime for legal persons so as to ensure consistency with the legal, institutional and operational responses to the requirements of the FATF, the Global Forum, the Mérida Convention and the EITI. ECOWAS countries are asked above all to ensure that corporate structures disclose adequate and accurate beneficial-ownership information at registration, and then to carry out comprehensive risk assessments and detailed typology studies, to strengthen the capacities of all stakeholders within the public architecture and the justice system at the level of the penal code, and finally to strengthen sanctions for non-compliance with beneficial-ownership disclosure obligations.

a6357.speaker: GIABA annual report (recommendations to GIABA itself)
a6357.speech: As for GIABA, it is recommended that it strengthen advocacy with OHADA and national legislators to integrate AML/CFT objectives, increase technical and financial assistance for national assessments of the risks of misuse of legal persons, and support ongoing legal and institutional reform initiatives in member countries by providing legal assistance and guidance in order to better align national laws and regulations with international standards.

a6462.speaker: 2021 Civic Media Lab Reporting Project (report/investigation)
a6462.speech: The investigation spotlighted the communities’ struggle with a lack of electricity for many decades.

a6462.speaker: Favour Oguibe, Founder of Luminous Life Foundation
a6462.speech: Said empowering underserved communities by providing them with clean energy solutions is the initiative’s core mission: “We did a lot of research, which led us to communities in Nigeria that do not have access to power, and the story popped up. Without this investigation, we may not have known about the situation in these places” ; “Other communities in Badagry do not have access to power, although the intervention which is our pilot project is in its first phase, we hope to expand the project in other areas subsequently”.

a6462.speaker: Faula Kamalideen, resident and beneficiary of the intervention
a6462.speech: Said the pump price of oil that has ballooned has made the solar lanterns even more useful and timely, adding that “the solar lanterns will help us see well at night and also assist the pupils study because when they return from school, it’s usually dark”.

a6462.speaker: Victoria Hungbo, beneficiary of the initiative
a6462.speech: “We deeply appreciate this gesture as it would also help sell our farm produce after dark” ; “We need a solar farm that can power a pumping system to help irrigate our farmlands and augment what these well-meaning people have brought us”.

a6462.speaker: Favour Oguibe, Founder of Luminous Life Foundation (on government and donors)
a6462.speech: Believes the lamps will provide an immediate solution to the power issue in both communities and help demonstrate how clean energy can make a difference and improve the overall quality of life ; noted that the intervention is an avenue to get word across to the Nigerian government that no community should live in darkness when the tools for change are within reach ; “Foreign organisations like the African Development Bank (AfDB), the United States Agency for International Development (USAID), and the World Bank recognise the major energy deficit Nigeria and other African countries face. These groups help tackle the energy shortcomings” ; “The government should make the most of investments from these bodies” ; added that setting up favourable policies and initiatives can foster an environment where a stable electricity supply becomes a reality for all citizens.

a6462.speaker: USAID (report, June 2024)
a6462.speech: According to a report by USAID in June 2024, 85 million Nigerians still live with no access to power, despite the presence of organisations like the Rural Electrification Agency (REA), Nigerian Electricity Regulatory Commission (NERC), Renewable Energy Association of Nigeria (REAN), among others.

a6493.speaker: John Bernon, director of the USAID health office in Benin
a6493.speech: Recalls that tuberculosis, although preventable and curable, remains one of the deadliest scourges, surpassing even HIV and malaria in its annual toll of human lives; recalls that in 2022 more than ten million people were affected worldwide and 1.3 million lost the battle against the disease; stresses that thanks to concerted efforts, including those of the “Stop Tuberculosis” programme supported by USAID, they have managed to save more than 75 million lives: “The training of the coming days is more than an opportunity, it is a call to action. Together, we have the power to make a significant difference in the lives of children affected by tuberculosis.”

a6493.speaker: Ange Dossou, representative of the Minister of Health of Benin
a6493.speech: Acknowledges that the fight against tuberculosis remains a major challenge among children; referring to World Health Organization figures, reports that out of 1,200,000 cases of tuberculosis detected in children worldwide each year only half are put on treatment, and that the gap is even greater among children under five who are unable to produce the sputum samples needed for diagnosis; notes that techniques such as gastric intubation are not easy to implement under routine conditions in African countries, and that the recent introduction of a stool-based technique offers hope of a significant improvement in screening: “This workshop therefore comes at just the right time to fill a gap, particularly at the level of French-speaking countries, since a number of English-speaking African countries were already able to benefit from training on this technique during 2023,” while encouraging participants to take full advantage of the workshop.

a6493.speaker: World Health Organization (WHO) figures
a6493.speech: Cited as the source of the claim that out of 1,200,000 cases of tuberculosis detected in children worldwide each year, only half are put on treatment.

a6688.speaker: Hersi Said, President of Yanga (Young Africans SC)
a6688.speech: Revealed at the club's general meeting that at the time of the great pressure for their striker Clement Mzize to be sold, the club received an offer of 2 million dollars, saying the last offer that came to the club was 2 million dollars (5 billion shillings) ; said their leadership blocked the sale, saying it would not have been easy to do that deal because Yanga still needed the strength of a striker ; "There were very many offers for our young man, but Yanga had no bad intentions; we knew what we wanted" ; "At the time of the pressure of those offers, Mzize called me and asked me, my president, tell me what the club's position is; do you want me to go or not to go? I told Mzize, calm down for now, get to work, keep playing with the national team, keep lighting it up and scoring goals; when you finish CHAN we will talk."

a6688.speaker: Hersi Said, President of Yanga (Young Africans SC)
a6688.speech: Said that after those finals Mzize's terms were improved and he became a well-paid player within the club ; "As we speak now, Mzize has two years remaining; he has completed one, and next year that is when we will look at how to sell him."

a6688.speaker: Clement Mzize, Yanga striker (speech reported by Hersi Said)
a6688.speech: "My president, tell me what the club's position is; do you want me to go or not to go?"

a6775.speaker: Tulio de Oliveira, Professor of bioinformatics and founding director of the Centre for Epidemic Response and Innovation (CERI), Stellenbosch University
